knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

## R Markdown

R Markdown is a file format for making dynamic documents with R. An R Markdown document is written in markdown (an easy-to-write plain text format) and contains chunks of embedded R code.

## Exploring the Data 

For this example, I will use the built-in `mtcars` dataset in R. This dataset contains information about different cars, including their fuel efficiency, horsepower, and weight. I want to explore the relationship between a car's weight and its miles per gallon (MPG).

## Loading and Summarizing the Dataset

The following code loads the dataset and calculates basic summary statistics.

```{r cars}
data(mtcars)

head(mtcars)

summary(mtcars$mpg)

mean(mtcars$mpg)
```
## Mathematical Expression

The mean is calculated by adding all observations and dividing by the total number of observations.

The formula for the mean is:

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n}
$$

In this equation, $\bar{x}$ represents the mean, $x_i$ represents each observation, and $n$ represents the number of observations.

Another example of an inline mathematical expression is $\alpha + \beta = \gamma$.

## Data Visualization

Next, I will create a scatterplot using `ggplot2` to explore the relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency.

```{r mtcars, echo=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Car Weight vs. Fuel Efficiency",
    x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
    y = "Miles Per Gallon"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

## Analysis

Based on the scatterplot, there appears to be a negative relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency. As the weight of a car increases, its miles per gallon generally decreases. This suggests that heavier cars tend to use more fuel than lighter cars.

## Reflection

Using R Markdown is different from writing a regular report because I can combine my explanations, code, and results in one place. Instead of copying graphs and statistics into a separate document, R Markdown allows me to generate everything together. I also like that I can make changes to my code and update the report by knitting it again. Although learning the formatting takes some practice, I think R Markdown is useful for organizing data analysis projects and making reports more reproducible.
